notes: Child benefit judicial review; Richards J's analysis of Schedule 10 discretion and guidance is complete.

enrichment.short_title: Ford v Revenue: child benefit split between separated parents

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Mr and Mrs Ford shared care of two children after divorce; Mr Ford originally received Child Benefit for both.
From May 2004 the Revenue paid Child Benefit for the younger child Michael to Mrs Ford while Ryan's benefit remained with Mr Ford.
Both parents were responsible for Michael under section 143; Schedule 10 paragraph 5 gave the Revenue a residual discretion where parents could not agree.
Mr Ford was on Income Support; Mrs Ford was in employment, but the Revenue split benefit one child each based on near-equal shared care.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Revenue's discretionary decision under Schedule 10 paragraph 5 to award Michael's Child Benefit to Mrs Ford.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Revenue lawfully looked at both children together, followed its internal guidance, and its decision was not irrational.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 5 discretion is unfettered and may take account of other children in the family; splitting Child Benefit one child per parent where care is nearly equal is not unlawful splitting under section 144(3), and Income Support impact may be considered without necessarily favouring the benefit claimant on benefits.
legal_issues: Whether the Revenue could consider other children when deciding Child Benefit for one child
Whether splitting benefit between parents breached section 144(3)
Whether the decision departed from internal guidance or ignored relevant factors
Whether the balancing exercise was Wednesbury irrational
linked_authorities: Gangadeen v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1998] Imm AR 106

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, facts and dismissal on multiple grounds are clearly reasoned.

notes: Detailed birth-injury negligence trial on preliminary issues; Bolam/Bolitho analysis and expert preference are comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: DA v Homerton: cerebral palsy and trial-of-scar caesarean delay
key_facts: The claimant suffered dyskinetic cerebral palsy from profound asphyxia shortly before caesarean delivery at 12.44 on 19 March 1994 at Homerton Hospital.
Delivery by 12.30 would likely have avoided brain damage; Mrs A was in trial of scar labour while Mr Ogueh operated on another patient in the only obstetric theatre.
The claimant alleged Mrs Lowe bleeped Mr Ogueh too late, should have called help earlier, and that Mr Ogueh should have reviewed Mrs A before theatre.
Fetal heart decelerations became critical around 12.00-12.10; crash bleep and emergency caesarean followed theatre unavailability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of liability and causation as preliminary issues in a clinical negligence claim for birth injury.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no negligence by midwives or obstetric staff on the three live issues; staff acted with due skill and care.
enrichment.ratio: On Bolam/Bolitho principles, a midwife was not negligent in failing to summon medical help before 12.03 where expert evidence supported her judgment, and a registrar may reasonably rely on midwives' silence and proceed with another emergency caesarean without first reviewing a trial-of-scar patient showing no earlier concern.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Lowe bleeped Mr Ogueh before the operation on Mrs O commenced
Whether Mrs Lowe should have called medical assistance earlier given CTG findings
Whether Mr Ogueh should have reviewed Mrs A before starting theatre
Application of Bolam and Bolitho to obstetric emergency management
linked_authorities: Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957] 1 WLR 582
Bolitho v City and Hackney Health Authority [1998] AC 232

confidence.notes: Long fact-finding judgment with clear conclusions on each causative allegation and strong expert reasoning.

notes: Mental Health Act s29 displacement appeal; Thorpe and Wall LJJ give detailed statutory and human-rights guidance.

enrichment.short_title: Lewis v Gibson: displacement of nearest relative under section 29
key_facts: M, a 34-year-old woman with Down's syndrome, was removed from her mother Brenda Lewis under section 135 in January 2003 after deteriorating care and euthanasia references.
Telford and Wrekin applied under section 29 to displace Mrs Lewis as nearest relative so guardianship could proceed; an interim order was made.
Judge Mitchell found M met section 7(2) criteria and that the mother's objection to guardianship was unreasonable.
The mother appealed, arguing misuse of the Mental Health Act, Article 8 breach, and that M no longer met severe mental impairment criteria.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from a county court decision confirming displacement of the nearest relative under section 29 of the Mental Health Act 1983.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; displacement upheld and the court gave guidance on relevant dates and patient participation following amendment of CCR Ord 49 r 12(3)(b).
enrichment.ratio: Section 29 criteria must be satisfied at both application and hearing, but the material date for jurisdiction is the application date by analogy with Re M; the court may prefer medical evidence on continuing severe mental impairment and need for guardianship, and patients should now be joined and represented in section 29 proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether the local authority should have used the inherent jurisdiction instead of the Mental Health Act
Whether M continued to meet section 7(2) severe mental impairment criteria at hearing
The relevant date for section 29(3)(c) unreasonableness
Compliance with Article 6 and Article 8 in section 29 procedure
linked_authorities: R (H) v Secretary of State for Health [2004] EWCA Civ 1609
Re M (a minor: care order: threshold conditions) [1994] 2 AC 424
Re F (Adult: Court's Jurisdiction) [2000] 2 FLR 512

notes: Case stated appeal on SO(A)A 1992 anonymity breach; Article 10 and Brown v UK analysis is complete.

enrichment.short_title: O'Riordan v DPP: Marie Claire breach of victim anonymity law
key_facts: Marie Claire published the name and photograph of a 12-year-old victim S in its January 2004 year-in-review edition after Studabaker was charged with inciting gross indecency.
Editor Paula O'Riordan pleaded guilty after the magistrate rejected no-case-to-answer; she said she would not have published had she known of the statutory restrictions.
The prosecution concerned publication likely to identify the victim of a listed sexual offence between 25 and 29 November 2003.
The appeal argued Article 10 required a section 5(5A) ignorance-of-allegation defence and that 'likely' was insufficiently precise.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Bow Street Magistrates' Court after conviction following a rejected submission of no case to answer.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; there was a case to answer, the restriction was necessary and proportionate, and the legislation was prescribed by law.
enrichment.ratio: On a causing-death/anonymity-type strict liability media offence, evidence that publication likely identified a protected victim suffices for a case to answer; Article 10 permits such restrictions to protect child victims, and Brown v United Kingdom supports proportionality without reading section 5(5A) into the unamended Act.
legal_issues: Whether there was a case to answer under sections 1 and 5 of the 1992 Act
Whether the statutory prohibition was necessary and proportionate under Article 10
Whether 'likely to lead members of the public to identify' was sufficiently prescribed by law
Effect of later insertion of section 5(5A)
index_terms: Attorney General v Greater Manchester Newspapers
linked_authorities: R v Shayler [2003] 1 AC 247
Brown v United Kingdom (2002) application 44223/98
Attorney General v Greater Manchester Newspapers Ltd (The Times, 7 December 2001)

confidence.notes: Facts admitted and human-rights challenge comprehensively rejected, though some parliamentary history of section 5(5A) was unavailable.

notes: Section 94(3) certification quashed on Karuna/LTTE asylum facts; borderline but reasoned judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Sinnarasa: quashing clearly unfounded asylum certification
key_facts: The claimant, a Sri Lankan Tamil, claimed asylum after arriving with false documents in June 2004.
She said she was an LTTE intelligence operative linked to Colonel Karuna's faction after the April 2004 schism and fled after colleagues were killed.
The Secretary of State refused asylum and certified the claim clearly unfounded under section 94(3), removing appeal rights while Sri Lanka was listed.
LTTE letters demanding her presence and expert evidence suggested she might fall within PS country guidance categories of at-risk Karuna supporters.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review, with limited permission, of refusal of asylum and section 94(3) clearly unfounded certification.
enrichment.outcome: Certification quashed; the claim was not so lacking in substance that an appeal was bound to fail, leaving the claimant free to appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Section 94(3) certification requires a high threshold that no legitimate view could succeed; PS country guidance leaves open that non-high-profile Karuna supporters may be at risk in Colombo, and the claimant's intelligence role, flight with senior defectors, LTTE summonses and expert evidence together raised a non-fanciful risk.
legal_issues: Whether an adjudicator could find the claimant within PS at-risk categories for Karuna supporters
Interpretation of PS country guidance on high-profile versus category-based targeting
The Bagdanavicius test for clearly unfounded certification
Whether sufficiency of state protection in Colombo negated the claim
linked_authorities: PS v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKIAT 00439
R v Bagdanavicius [2004] INLR 163
NM and Others (Somalia) Country Guidance [2005] UKIAT 00076

confidence.notes: Judge expressly treated facts as assumed for certification review; outcome is clear though merits remain untested.

notes: Landmark performing-edition copyright appeal; detailed subsistence and infringement reasoning from three judges.

enrichment.short_title: Hyperion v Sawkins: copyright in baroque performing editions
key_facts: Dr Lionel Sawkins created scholarly performing editions of three out-of-copyright Lalande grands motets with extensive editorial corrections and re-created parts.
Hyperion recorded Ex Cathedra performing from Sawkins' scores on the CD 'Music for the Sun King' without consent and denied copyright royalties.
Patten J held each edition was an original musical work, had been substantially copied, and Sawkins' paternity right under section 77 was breached.
Hyperion argued the recordings were of Lalande's music, not new composition, and that figured bass and editorial marks were not 'music'.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a High Court judgment finding copyright infringement and breach of moral rights in modern performing editions of historical music.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on subsistence, infringement, Paillard-edition originality and moral rights; Sawkins' editions were protectable original musical works.
enrichment.ratio: A performing edition of public-domain music may be an original musical work where the editor's skill and labour produces a playable score affecting the sounds performed; Walter v Lane applies, and editorial interventions including figured bass and performance directions can constitute music for copyright purposes without creating a monopoly in the underlying composer’s work.
legal_issues: Whether performing editions of out-of-copyright music are original musical works
Whether Hyperion substantially reproduced the editions in its sound recordings
Whether Sawkins unconsciously copied the Paillard edition of La Grande Piece Royale
Whether section 77 required stronger authorship identification on the CD
linked_authorities: Walter v Lane [1900] AC 539
Interlego AG v Tyco Industries Inc [1988] RPC 343
Ladbroke (Football) Ltd v William Hill (Football) Ltd [1964] 1 WLR 273

confidence.notes: Full appellate treatment of subsistence, infringement and moral rights with detailed findings of fact preserved from trial.

notes: Commercial Court off-hire clause judgment; detention and proviso analysis follows Jalagouri closely.

enrichment.short_title: Hyundai v Furness Withy: off hire during USCG security boarding
key_facts: The Doric Pride was time chartered for a US Gulf to South Korea grain voyage under an NYPE form with clause 85 off-hire provisions.
On first call to the United States she was designated a High Interest Vessel and ordered to wait offshore for US Coast Guard security inspection at New Orleans.
She waited from 09.20 on 20 February until inspection cleared at 12.45 on 26 February 2004, during which the Mississippi was also closed after collisions.
Charterers placed disputed hire in escrow; Owners argued no detention, or that the proviso and implied indemnity applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court dispute on construction of an off-hire clause in a single-trip time charter.
enrichment.outcome: Charterers succeeded; the vessel was off hire for the full waiting period and the clause 85 proviso and implied indemnity did not apply.
enrichment.ratio: A vessel is 'detained' under an off-hire clause when a physical or geographical constraint prevents performance of charter service, following The Jalagouri, even if she could sail elsewhere; a period off-hire clause suspends hire until release without net-loss accounting, and generic US Gulf post-9/11 inspection risk was accepted by Owners rather than caused by nomination of New Orleans.
legal_issues: Whether USCG inspection orders amounted to detention under clause 85
Whether river closure superseded USCG detention from 21 February
Whether the proviso made detention occasioned by calling port apply
Whether Owners could recover hire via an implied indemnity under clause 8
linked_authorities: The Jalagouri [1999] 1 Lloyd's Rep 903
The Mareva A/S [1977] 1 Lloyd's Rep 368
The Island Archon [1994] 2 Lloyd's Rep 227

confidence.notes: Clear commercial construction judgment with agreed facts on timing and no extra-expense claim.

notes: Section 287 local plan challenge; Ground 1 fails, Ground 2 partially succeeds on green belt map error.

enrichment.short_title: Persimmon v Stevenage: local plan conformity and green belt map
key_facts: Hertfordshire Structure Plan Policy 8 allocated about 1,000 dwellings at Stevenage West west of the A1(M), excluding land from the Green Belt.
Stevenage Borough Council adopted a replacement local plan Policy H2 identifying the land but safeguarding it pending reassessment of strategic justification.
Developers challenged whether the caveated policy was in general conformity with the Structure Plan and whether the Green Belt boundary near Norton Green was lawfully adopted.
The local plan inspector recommended the caveat wording; the council adopted it despite developer objections.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 287 application to quash parts of an adopted replacement local plan for non-conformity with the structure plan and procedural defect.
enrichment.outcome: Ground 1 failed; Policy H2 was in general conformity. Ground 2 succeeded and the Green Belt proposals map near Norton Green was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: General conformity allows a local plan to reproduce a structure plan allocation subject to a qualification about reassessment where it still contemplates achievement in the plan period; however failure to consider a Green Belt boundary objection is an error requiring quashing, after which the affected land reverts to unallocated status rather than automatic green belt restoration.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'general conformity' between local and structure plans
Whether Policy H2's safeguard caveat departed materially from Structure Plan Policy 8
Whether the inspector's failure to address a Green Belt objection invalidated adoption
Discretionary relief after partial quashing under section 287
linked_authorities: J S Bloor Ltd v Swindon Borough Council [2001] EWHC Admin 966
Charles Church Developments Ltd v South Northamptonshire District Council (1999)
Persimmon Homes v North Hertfordshire District Council [2001] EWHC 565

confidence.notes: Split outcome clearly explained though planning policy context was transitional between 1990 and 2004 Acts.

notes: Criminal appeal on cocaine evidence admissibility in death by dangerous driving; McBride/Woodward applied.

enrichment.short_title: R v Pleydell: cocaine evidence in dangerous driving death
key_facts: The appellant lost control at about 44 mph on Carew Road, Eastbourne, colliding with a parked car and killing his passenger.
Blood taken about three hours later showed cocaine and cannabis; the Crown relied on recent cocaine use, not cannabis.
The trial judge admitted the cocaine evidence over defence objection based on R v Woodward principles.
The appellant denied taking cocaine shortly before driving but admitted occasional prior use and lied initially in interview.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal against conviction for causing death by dangerous driving after a mid-trial ruling admitting drug evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; admission of cocaine evidence was justified and the conviction stood.
enrichment.ratio: In causing death by dangerous driving, evidence that a driver recently consumed cocaine is admissible where it tends to show adverse effect or likely impairment, unlike mere proof of drinking; unchanged cocaine in blood demonstrates recent use and, with expert evidence of impairment capacity and the defendant's lies, was probative rather than merely prejudicial.
legal_issues: Admissibility of drug-use evidence in dangerous driving prosecutions
Application of McBride, Thorpe and Woodward to Class A drugs
Whether absence of quantitative analysis rendered evidence inadmissible
Distinction between alcohol consumption and recent cocaine use
linked_authorities: R v Woodward [1995] 2 Cr App R 388
McBride (1961) 45 Cr App R 262
R v Thorpe (1972) 56 Cr App R 296

confidence.notes: Appeal turned on a discrete evidential ruling with full trial context and clear appellate approval.

notes: Judicial review of Crown Court bail refusal; short but complete Wednesbury analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Galliano: judicial review of Crown Court bail refusal
key_facts: The claimant received a combination order of 40 hours' community service and 12 months' rehabilitation for a dishonest theft from a vulnerable elderly victim.
He attended his first community service appointment drunk, breaching the order, and was brought back for resentencing.
Judge Lever adjourned for reports but refused bail for four weeks, citing substantial risk of further offences on bail.
Four of the claimant's last five convictions had been committed while on bail, though he had attended court voluntarily.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Crown Court judge's refusal of bail pending resentencing for breach of a community sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the bail refusal was not irrational and the risk-of-further-offences ground was a proper basis to refuse bail.
enrichment.ratio: High Court review of Crown Court bail decisions is limited to Wednesbury irrationality since direct bail appeals to the High Court were abolished; a judge may refuse bail where breach of a non-custodial sentence and prior offences on bail create a substantial risk of further offending pending resentencing likely to result in custody.
legal_issues: Scope of judicial review of Crown Court bail decisions
Whether refusal on risk of further offences was irrational
Effect of prior convictions committed on bail
Presumption in favour of bail on resentencing adjournment

confidence.notes: Short judgment but complete on the limited review standard and factual basis for bail refusal.
